text: Chapter 6 teaches the core arranging techniques for transforming jazz standards into complete solo guitar pieces, beginning with walking bass construction (root on beat 1, diatonic or chromatic approach note on beat 4, interior notes chosen from scales, chromatics, or arpeggios) and layering shell voicings rhythmically on the downbeat or '& of 1' to maintain drive. The chapter moves through melodic harmonization strategies — diatonic passing chords sourced from the chord dictionary and chromatic approach chords using the same voicing shape moved one fret — before introducing substitution techniques that define modern jazz guitar voice-leading: tritone substitution (replacing any chord with one a tritone away, valid because guide tones swap places while remaining common tones), relative substitution (vi for I), chord iii substitution, and the minor-7-for-dominant rule (using the iim7 of the dominant). The arrangement framework also covers chord addition (inserting substitutions to expand harmonic rhythm) and the ii/V interchangeability Joe Pass famously employed. Throughout, the chapter emphasizes the solo guitarist's freedom to apply these techniques liberally without ensemble constraints, and prioritizes the use of diads over octaves for a 'richer, more authentic' jazz sound. The load-bearing concepts are walking bass as functional drive-keeper during long melody notes, guide tones as the harmonic mechanism underlying substitutions, and the systematic substitution rules that let the player extend and personalize existing changes.
